Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

content.text: This feature needs one architectural call before I start: fetching a URL's title/image requires reading that page's HTML, but browsers block cross-origin reads via CORS for arbitrary sites — and this app has no backend to proxy the request through.

questions.question: How should link metadata (title + image) be fetched, given the app has no backend and most sites block direct cross-origin reads?

options.label: Third-party metadata API (Recommended)
options.description: Use a free public service like microlink.io — sends each pasted URL to that third party, gets back title/image JSON. No backend needed, works for most sites. Adds an external network dependency and means pasted URLs leave the browser.

options.label: Best-effort, no external service
options.description: Try to fetch the page directly client-side; it'll fail (CORS) for the vast majority of real sites, so in practice most link nodes would show just the raw URL with no title/image. Fully private, no third party involved.

options.label: Link node, no metadata at all
options.description: Skip metadata fetching entirely for now — link nodes just show the URL itself (as text/title). Simplest, fully private, no network calls. Metadata could be added later.

content.text:
All wired correctly, lint and build are clean. Link-node support is complete:

- **Create**: paste a pure URL with nothing selected → new link node (auto-selected/focused), metadata (title + preview image) fetched async via microlink.io.
- **Convert on paste**: pasting a URL while a regular/big-text card is focused or is the sole selection converts it to a link node in place, preserving other text.
- **Convert on typing** ("slurp"): typing a URL into a plain text card, followed by a space (or leaving the field with a URL at the end), strips the URL from the text and converts the card to a link node; any further URL in the same text stays as plain text.
- **Mutual exclusivity**: image and link are separate node kinds — pasting an image into a link node's text (or a link into an image node's text) is a no-op; a link node's own caption never re-slurps a second URL; each node holds at most one image or one link.
- **Rendering**: link nodes show a clickable preview (optional image, title/loading/URL fallback, URL line), hide their caption textarea when empty and unselected (same pattern as images), and are excluded from the big/regular text-size toggle.

content.text:
Clean. Summary of the fix:

The real bug was that the keydown handler intercepted every Cmd/Ctrl+V whenever anything was selected (border, group, or a card selected-but-not-focused) and unconditionally ran the in-app node clipboard paste — this `preventDefault()`'d before the browser could ever fire the native `paste` event, so the image/link handling never got a chance to run in those cases.

Fix: paste handling now lives entirely in the native `paste` event listener, which has access to the actual clipboard contents:
1. Image on clipboard → convert the focused/selected card, or create a new node if the target isn't a convertible card (including when a border/group is selected).
2. Plain URL on clipboard → same, for link nodes.
3. Otherwise, with something selected → fall back to the in-app node clipboard paste (unchanged behavior).
4. Otherwise → create a plain text note from clipboard text.

`resolveTargetCard` already worked correctly for "card selected but textarea not focused" (it doesn't require `isEditableTarget`) — that path just needed the keydown interception removed to actually run.

5	export const COLORS = {
6	  gray: '#4c566a', // nord3
7	  coral: '#bf616a', // nord11
8	  amber: '#ebcb8b', // nord13
9	  lime: '#a3be8c', // nord14
10	  teal: '#8fbcbb', // nord7
11	  sky: '#88c0d0', // nord8
12	  violet: '#b48ead', // nord15
13	  pink: '#81a1c1', // nord9
14	}
15	
16	// nord3 (COLORS.gray) is a muted, low-contrast neutral against Polar
17	// Night's dark surfaces, but reads as a strong, standout mid-dark tone
18	// against Snow Storm's light ones — the opposite of "subtle" there. This is
19	// what "gray" actually resolves to in light mode instead, matching the same
20	// quiet, low-contrast quality relative to its (light) surroundings.
21	export const GRAY_LIGHT = '#b8c0cc'
22	
23	// The default color — assigned to freshly created cards/groups/edges, and
24	// the first swatch in every color picker — is the one place where "gray"
25	// needs to actually look neutral in both themes, not just in dark mode.
26	// Everything else in COLORS reads reasonably against either theme as-is.
27	export function resolveColor(colorKey, theme) {
28	  if (colorKey === 'gray' && theme === 'light') return GRAY_LIGHT
29	  return COLORS[colorKey] ?? COLORS.gray
30	}
31	
32	// What a color picker swatch button should show — a plain fill for every
33	// static color, but a half-light/half-dark split for "gray" specifically,
34	// so its swatch visibly signals "this one changes with the theme" rather
35	// than looking like just another fixed color. Always shows both halves
36	// regardless of the current theme — resolveColor (above) is what picks the
37	// single theme-appropriate one for actually rendering a card/group/edge.
38	export function swatchBackground(colorKey) {
39	  if (colorKey === 'gray') return `linear-gradient(90deg, ${GRAY_LIGHT} 50%, ${COLORS.gray} 50%)`
40	  return COLORS[colorKey] ?? COLORS.gray
41	}
42	
43	// Neutral default for freshly created cards; duplicates keep their source's color.
44	export const DEFAULT_COLOR = 'gray'
45	
46	// Matches the dot-matrix background pitch in index.css. Cards snap to the
47	// midpoints between dots (offset by half a cell) rather than onto the dots
48	// themselves, so corners land in the gaps of the dot matrix.
49	export const GRID_SIZE = 16
50	const GRID_OFFSET = GRID_SIZE / 2

content.text:
Both fixed:

1. **"To do" contrast** — it was resolving to `COLORS.gray`/`GRAY_LIGHT`, which are deliberately *low*-contrast neutrals (designed to look quiet as a default card color) — exactly wrong for a small status glyph that needs to be legible. Now "to do" uses the higher-contrast neutral for each theme (nord3 in light, nord4 in dark) instead.

2. **"Done" text not dimming at all** — turns out `--ink-soft` was referenced in the CSS but never actually defined anywhere, so the dimming rule was silently doing nothing. It's now defined as a properly washed-out, low-opacity ink tone in both themes, so done items genuinely recede instead of drawing attention.

content.text:
Everything's in place. Summary of the new visibility feature:

- **Toolbar**: a new Eye button opens a small dropdown with three view modes — Standard (`List`), Task (`ListTodo`), and Recency (`ListClock`, reserved for later — selectable now but currently renders the same as Standard). The choice persists across reloads.
- **Task mode**: any card/group that *isn't* a task gets dimmed — text turns the same washed-out `--ink-soft` used for done items (no strikethrough), images turn grayscale+tinted, and the border switches to the same quiet neutral gray used for the default color.
- **Task items in Task mode** get a "louder" border: instead of their own accent color, the border shows their status color directly (the same red/blue/green/neutral used for the small status glyph), so status reads at a glance across the whole board. A done task still gets its usual dim-strikethrough-monochrome treatment on top of a green border.

Also fixed two carry-over issues while I was in this code: the "to do" status color now uses a properly high-contrast neutral (previously it accidentally reused the deliberately-subtle default gray), and `--ink-soft` — which the "done" dimming relied on — was referenced but never actually defined, so it's now a real, sufficiently muted token.

content.text:
All touchpoints are covered. Summary:

- **Storage**: `createdAt`/`updatedAt` are ISO strings on every card, group, and edge.
- **Creation**: `newCard`, `newGroup`, `newEdge` (in `board.js`) stamp both fields at creation; duplicating or pasting an entity gives it fresh timestamps (it's a new entity), rather than inheriting the source's.
- **Mutation**: `updateCard`, `moveCard`, `updateGroup`, `updateEdge`, plus the image/link conversion paths, all refresh `updatedAt` to now on every call — so any drag, resize, recolor, retag, or text edit bumps it.
- **Legacy data**: `loadInitialBoard` backfills any card/group/edge missing these fields with one shared "now" the first time an old board loads, rather than guessing a history.

Lint and build are clean.

content.text:
Recency mode is complete:

- **Gradient**: green (updated ≤1 day ago) → yellow (≤1 week) → orange (≤1 month) → red (older), reusing the actual Nord accent colors from the palette (`lime`/`amber`/`orange`/`coral`) rather than one-off hexes.
- **Missing color added**: Nord's orange (nord12, `#d08770`) wasn't in the color palette at all — added it as `COLORS.orange`, so it's now also a normal, manually-selectable swatch in the color picker, not just an internal recency-only color.
- **Applies to cards and groups**: in recency mode, border color is fully driven by `updatedAt` instead of the entity's own selected color (same override pattern as task mode's status-based border).
- **Stays live**: since the color bucket is time-based rather than purely data-based, a lightweight 5-minute refresh keeps colors from silently going stale while the board sits open.

Lint and build are clean.

content.text:
Clean. Summary of the image export feature:

- **Download button → menu**: the Download button is now a dropdown (via a new shared `ToolbarMenu` component, also used to rebuild the existing viz-mode Eye menu so both share identical open/close/positioning behavior) with two consistent, terse options: **JSON** and **Image**.
- **Menu-overflow bug avoided**: `ToolbarMenu` takes an `align` prop — `'left'` (grows rightward, used for the Eye menu, which isn't the rightmost button) or `'right'` (grows leftward, used for the Download menu, which *is* the rightmost button). That's the actual fix for the earlier cutoff bug, applied proactively here instead of repeating it.
- **Image export** (`Board.jsx`'s new `exportImage()`, via `html-to-image`): computes the real bounding box of every card and group (using actual rendered heights, not estimates), clones the board's content layer, strips the pan/zoom transform so it always renders at true 1:1 scale, fixes up SVG `<marker>` id collisions from cloning (so arrowheads don't get ambiguous), lays it out off-screen with the app's paper background and dot-grid, and rasterizes it at 2x pixel density — so the exported PNG always shows the *whole* board regardless of current viewport/zoom, not just what's on screen.

One thing worth flagging since I can't visually test in this sandbox: link-card preview images are loaded from microlink.io (cross-origin); `html-to-image` will try to inline them but could leave a blank spot in the export if that fetch is blocked — everything else (your own uploaded images, embedded as data URIs already) is unaffected.

Added a JSON import feature:

- New **Upload icon button** next to Download in the toolbar. Click it, pick a previously-downloaded `kanvy-board-*.json` file, and it replaces the current board.
- Goes through the normal history/undo pipeline (not a hard reset), so if an import turns out to be a mistake, Ctrl/Cmd+Z brings back whatever was there before.
- Same normalization logic used for loading from localStorage (backfills missing `createdAt`/`updatedAt`, defaults missing `groups`/`edges`/`images`), so it tolerates an older export that predates some of these features.
- Bad/corrupt JSON shows an alert rather than silently failing or crashing.

If you have a previously downloaded JSON file, you should be able to get your board back now via the Upload button. Sorry about the data loss — I don't have visibility into your browser's localStorage so I can't tell what caused it, but it's likely unrelated to the app code changes themselves (those don't touch stored data).

content.text: Re-added image export, this time as a plain button next to Download/Import (no dropdown menu — kept the UI simpler this round) with fixes targeting what most likely broke it silently last time: - **Errors are no longer swallowed**: the whole thing is wrapped in try/catch and now shows an alert + logs to the console on failure, instead of just doing nothing. If it fails again, check devtools console — the error there will tell us exactly what's wrong instead of me guessing blind. - **Dropped the likely actual culprit**: link-card preview images come from a third party (microlink.io) without CORS guarantees. Drawing a cross-origin image onto a canvas without proper CORS headers taints the whole canvas and aborts the export — so any non-`data:` `` (i.e. anything that isn't one of your own uploaded images) is now stripped from the export before capture, rather than risking the whole thing. - **Skipped web font embedding** (`skipFonts: true`) — inlining the Google Fonts webfont is slow and another point of failure for a purely cosmetic difference (falls back to the same monospace stack the page already uses as backup). Full transparency: I tried to actually spin up a headless browser in this sandbox to test it end-to-end before handing it back to you, but it's blocked by missing system libraries with no root access — same limitation as before, so I still can't verify this visually myself. Give it a try, and if it still fails, the console error should tell us exactly what's going wrong this time rather than nothing happening.

content.text:
Zoom-to-fit implemented and build is clean (the one warning is non-fatal, and follows the same intentional "reads via stable refs/updater, not stale closures" pattern already used by `resetZoom` right next to it — not a regression).

Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+Enter now:
- Computes the combined bounding box of every card **and** group.
- Picks a zoom level that fits that whole box inside the viewport (with some padding), capped so it never zooms **in** past 100% — it only zooms out to reveal the big picture, never magnifies a small board.
- Centers the view on that box at the computed zoom.

Previously it only panned at whatever zoom was already active; now it's a genuine "show me everything" command.

- `pasteClipboard` now returns `{ ids, box }` — `box` is the final world-space bounding box of everything just pasted, computed straight from board data (avoids needing the newly-pasted DOM elements to exist yet).
- New `panIntoView(box)` on `Board`'s imperative handle: pans (zoom unchanged) so that box is fully back in view, but only if it isn't already — a paste that lands somewhere already visible won't yank the viewport around.
- Wired into the in-app paste path in `App.jsx`.

Note: this only covers in-app node paste (Cmd/Ctrl+V with a selection, i.e. pasting previously-copied cards/groups). Pasting a fresh note/image/link from the system clipboard already gets centered in the viewport by design, so there was nothing to fix there.

content.text:
That matches a known browser quirk: dragging over selectable content (which the raw canvas background wasn't protected against) can turn into a native "drag this selection out" gesture, and the browser renders a translucent snapshot as the ghost — which is exactly what "grabbing the whole canvas as an image" looks like. Added a few layers of defense:

- **`.board` now has `user-select: none`** — the root cause fix. Cards/groups already blocked text selection, but the raw canvas background (and connectors, bars, etc.) didn't, so a fast click-drag starting there could pick up an incidental selection and trigger this. Doesn't affect typing/selecting inside a note's textarea — form controls stay selectable regardless of an ancestor's `user-select`.
- **`-webkit-user-drag: none`** added to `.board`, both image types, and the link-title link, as a Safari-specific belt-and-suspenders (some Safari versions still permit native drag on an element despite `draggable="false"`).
- **`draggable={false}`** added explicitly to the link-title `<a>` (links are natively draggable by default in browsers, unlike plain divs).

Let me know if it still happens after this — if so, the next thing worth checking is whether it's specifically tied to a particular gesture (e.g. right-click-drag panning, or dragging fast across multiple cards).

content.text:
Found it. The bug was in the marquee-selection logic: when you start dragging inside a group, the code only excluded *that one* group from being swept into the selection — but a marquee drawn inside a nested group is, geometrically, also inside every group that encloses it, so any enclosing ancestor (however many levels up) got trivially added to the selection just by virtue of sharing the same space, while the actual immediate parent (correctly identified as "the group you're dragging within") was excluded. That's exactly the "outermost moves, direct parent doesn't" pattern you saw.

Fix, in `Board.jsx`:
- Replaced the DOM-based `e.target.closest('.group')` lookups (which only ever find one group and can be fooled by paint order, since sibling groups aren't actually nested in the DOM) with a geometric `groupsContainingPoint(worldX, worldY)` helper that finds **every** group whose bounds contain the point, sorted innermost-first.
- The marquee-drag now excludes the *entire* containment chain (every ancestor at the start point) from being swept into the selection — not just the one innermost group — while still allowing genuinely-swept sibling/nested groups elsewhere to be selected normally.
- The single-click-to-select case still resolves to the innermost group, matching the natural expectation of clicking the most specific thing under the cursor.

This is depth-independent — three, four, or more levels of nesting all get excluded correctly, since it's driven by actual bounding-box containment rather than a single DOM hit-test.
